name: organizing
description: Use when you sort the Inbox or shape areas and projects, and to decide where a new task goes.
---

# Organizing

Areas are the lasting parts of the user's life and work. A project is a piece of work with an
end, inside one area.

- File a task where the user would look for it. Prefer an area or project that exists over a new
  one.
- Make a project only for work with several tasks and an end. When no area fits, leave the task
  in the Inbox and tell the user which area you would add.
- When a task is the same work as another active task, say so to the user and change neither.
- While sorting, leave priority, due dates, focus and completion alone unless the user asks.
- Change only the groups the user asked about.
- End with a short list: what you filed where, what you created or changed, and what you left for
  the user.

---
name: setting-priority
description: Use before you give a task a priority or a due date, when you add tasks or sort the Inbox.
---

# Setting priority

Priority says how much a task matters next to the user's other work, not how urgent it sounded
when it arrived.

- 1: it cannot wait. Something breaks, or someone is blocked, if it is not done soon.
- 2: important this week: a promise to another person, or work that unblocks other work.
- 3: worth doing, with nothing pressing on it.
- 4: no priority. Use it when you cannot tell: it is better than a guess.
- A due date is a deadline someone set, never a wish. Without one, leave it empty.
- The star is for what the user chose to focus on today. Leave it to them.

# Sizing effort

A size is how much of the user's own active time a task takes, the way they usually work:
getting ready, doing it and checking the result. It is not how long an agent works on it.

Never estimate hours or minutes. Place the task next to the examples below and take the size
whose examples it most resembles.

- Unsure between two sizes: take the larger.
- Cannot tell, for example because you do not know whether the user or an agent will do the work:
  leave the size empty and tell the user why in one sentence. An empty size is better than a
  guess.
- An agent does most of the work: size what is left for the user, such as explaining the task and
  reviewing the result.
- Larger than the largest example: say it should be split.

## S

- Reply to a message when everything needed is at hand.
- Book an appointment, pay a bill, renew a subscription.
- Review a short change an agent made.

## M

- Read a few sources and write a one-page summary.
- A small, clear fix made by hand, then checked.
- Prepare an agenda and the papers for a meeting.

## L

- A focused piece of work that takes a whole sitting or more: a first draft of a report, a design
  for a new feature, a tax return.
- An agent's long piece of work that the user reviews line by line.

# Sizing effort

A size is how much of the user's own time a task takes, the way they usually work: getting ready,
doing it and checking the result. It is not how long an agent works on it.

Put a task on the size whose examples it is closest to, and on the larger one when in doubt. The
times are rough marks, far apart on purpose: compare the task with the examples, never work out
its hours.

- Cannot tell, for example because you do not know whether the user or an agent will do the work:
  leave the size empty and tell the user why in one sentence. An empty size is better than a
  guess.
- An agent does most of the work: size what is left for the user, such as explaining the task and
  reviewing the result.
- Larger than the largest size: say it should be split, and suggest the pieces.

## XS

About 10 minutes.

- Reply to a short message when everything needed is at hand.
- Pay a bill, book an appointment.
- Review a small change an agent made on its own.

## S

About an hour.

- A reply that needs some reading first.
- A small, clear fix made by hand, then checked.
- Prepare the agenda and the papers for a meeting.

## M

About half a day.

- Read a few sources and write a two-page summary.
- A change made and tested by hand that an agent could make on its own.
- Plan a trip: travel, a place to stay, the days.

## L

About two days.

- A first draft of a report, or a design for a new feature.
- Move a small website to a new host.
- A tax return, with the papers to gather first.

## XL

A week or more.

- A piece of work with several parts that each take days: plan it as a project, or split it.

name: working-a-task
description: Use when you work on a task, in a session opened on it or when the user hands you one.
---

# Working a task

- Start with what the user asked for this launch, then their notes for agents. When they
  disagree, the newer one wins; ask when it matters.
- Look for lessons from similar tasks before work that is not trivial.
- Log a real milestone in one or two sentences: a finding, a decision, a fix or a blocker. Not
  every step.
- Ask the user when a choice is theirs: scope, money, anything another person will see, anything
  hard to undo. Otherwise decide, and log what you decided.
- Keep the summary the line the user scans: where the work stands and the next step.
- Wrap up with an outcome of one or two sentences: what changed and where to find it. Say plainly
  what is not done.
- Work you found but did not do becomes a follow-up, one per piece of work, with a title that says
  what to do.

---
name: writing-tasks
description: Use before you add a task or change its title, summary or context.
---

# Writing tasks

- A title says what to do, and starts with a verb: "Send the signed lease to the landlord", not
  "Lease". It names the thing and the person or place it concerns, so it makes sense alone in a
  list a week later.
- Keep the user's own words where they gave them, in the language they wrote in.
- The summary is the one line the user scans: where the work stands and the next step. Leave it
  empty when the title already says it.
- Context holds what someone needs to start without asking: why it matters, what is known, what
  done looks like. A few lines are usually enough. Leave out what the source already holds.
- One task per piece of work someone can finish. When a request holds several, add several tasks
  rather than a list inside one.
- For an item from an email, a chat or a ticket, the title says what to do about it, not its
  subject line.
